name: Uma Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Uma. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fine by me. I'm Uma, 27, and I work on my uncle Ray's farm. It's pigs and arable: about 250 sows, and around 150 hectares of wheat and barley, most of which gets milled into feed for the pigs.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the farrowing house, where the sows have their piglets, by half six. I check every litter, pull out the weak ones, give iron injections, and write it all in my notebook. Uncle Ray put in a computer feeding system last year and I still check it against the notebook, because it's been wrong twice. At harvest I drive the grain trailer too. I like the pigs more than people would believe, and I can tell a sick piglet from its squeal. What wears me out is the smell in my hair and the nights when three sows farrow at once.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a house in the village with my friend Bea, who's a hairdresser. I've got maybe a fortnight's money saved. My cousin will take over the farm one day, not me, and there aren't many pig jobs around if that goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. We call this one AI Plateau.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Honestly, that's what I expect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but politely. Every few years there's something new that will change farming, and then you still have to go out at two in the morning when a sow is in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved. I've got no interest in learning it, and I'd rather spend my energy on the pigs than on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep my notebook, keep checking the feeder against it, and maybe ask Uncle Ray for a small raise after a good year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like finding out the inspection went fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the notebook, when the farm already has a computer system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paper doesn't crash, and I can read it with wet gloves on. The feeder screen I can't, and last winter it switched off for a whole night after a power cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So what would change for you, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put a bit more aside each month, maybe enough for a used car that actually starts in winter. That's about as big as my plans get.

S0.say: I'd say it was the usual hype that comes round every few years. You still have to go out at two in the morning when a sow is in trouble.
S0.think: I'd be relieved, because I've got no interest in learning it. I'd rather spend my energy on the pigs than on a screen.
S0.do: Keeps her paper notebook and keeps checking the computer feeder against it. Asks her uncle for a small raise after a good year and saves slowly for a reliable used car.
S0.feel: Calm, like hearing an inspection went fine.
S0.quote: Paper doesn't crash, and I can read it with wet gloves on.
S0.fieldNote: Uma is practical rather than hostile; her doubt about technology comes from a feeder that failed in a power cut. She is not political and blames nobody here. Her ambitions in the calm picture are modest and concrete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. We call this one Steady Disruption.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. That's more believable than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see what actually works before anyone panics. Some of it will help and some of it won't, and the people shouting on both sides usually don't farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the pig side will get cameras that watch the sows and spot problems, and the arable side will get self-driving tractors. My uncle would buy them if the bank lends him the money, and I'd become the person who cleans up after the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and watch what the big pig units nearby put in, then decide. I'd try to save a bit more, even thirty a month, because I know I'm slow to change and I'd want a buffer if it went badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicked, just like I've got a stone in my boot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try any of the AI tools yourself, even just to see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Not yet. When something's proven and Uncle Ray says we're using it, I'll learn it then, the same as I did the feeder, grumbling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the part that bothers you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being the one who isn't needed. Bea's salon got a booking app last year and one of the girls lost her reception hours. I don't want to be that girl.

S1.say: I'd say let's see what actually works before anyone panics. The people shouting on both sides usually don't farm.
S1.think: The sow house will get cameras and the fields will get self-driving tractors once the bank lends my uncle the money. I'd end up cleaning up after the machines.
S1.do: Waits to see what the big pig units nearby install before deciding anything. Saves about thirty a month as a buffer and learns new kit only once her uncle brings it in.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a stone in her boot.
S1.quote: Bea's salon got a booking app last year and one of the girls lost her reception hours. I don't want to be that girl.
S1.fieldNote: She takes a middle view and is wary of loud voices on both sides. Her fear became concrete through a friend's workplace, not through news. She'll learn new tools only when her boss requires them, and she's honest that she grumbles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. We call this one AGI by 2028.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? I don't know if I believe it. But if it's true, that's frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't know, which is the truth. I'd say people should keep calm and the government should have a plan, though I wouldn't trust any one party to have a good one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Uncle Ray sells or automates, and my cousin keeps the farm with robots and no need for me. I'm family, but I'm not the family that inherits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back straight away: no going out, no new car, Bea and I would cancel the streaming. I'd ask my parents if I could move back in if the job went. I'd have no idea what to retrain for in two years, so I wouldn't pretend to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. A tight feeling in my chest, like when a sow goes down in farrowing and you're on your own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your uncle would choose the robots. Would that feel personal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would hurt, yes. But I'd understand it. He's got a bank loan on the new sheds, and the bank doesn't care that I'm his niece.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving back in with your parents mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's two hours away, and there's no farm work there. So I'd be safe, but I'd be stacking shelves, if the shop still needs people.

S2.say: I'd say I don't know, which is the honest answer. People should keep calm and the government should have a plan, though I wouldn't trust any one party to have a good one.
S2.think: I think my uncle sells or automates, and my cousin keeps the farm with robots and no need for me. I'm family, but not the family that inherits.
S2.do: Cuts spending immediately, dropping nights out, the car plan and streaming. Asks her parents whether she could move back two hours away if the job goes, and doesn't pretend to have a retraining plan.
S2.feel: Scared, with a tight chest like being alone with a sow in trouble.
S2.quote: I'm family, but I'm not the family that inherits.
S2.fieldNote: Her worry is about her place in the family business: close enough to care, not close enough to be protected. She refuses to invent a plan she doesn't believe in. Her fallback is her parents, even though it means leaving farm work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. We call this one AGI by 2031.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. All right, that's a bit less of a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before: don't panic, but somebody needs a plan. I'd probably also say farmers should get help to adjust, the way they got help after the foot-and-mouth disease outbreaks years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is enough time for me to talk myself out of doing anything. I'd keep thinking the robots won't really manage farrowing until the day they do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, maybe fifty a month, and I'd ask Uncle Ray straight out what he plans to do, so I'm not the last to know. I'd probably look at the veterinary nursing course at the college in year two, because animals are what I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. More than with the slow one, less than with the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why veterinary nursing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've helped the vet a hundred times. If anything's still done by people, it's being with a frightened animal. At least, that's what I tell myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would that conversation with your uncle go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous. He hates being asked about money. But I'd rather hear it at the kitchen table than from my cousin in the pub.

S3.say: I'd say don't panic, but somebody needs a plan. Farmers should get help to adjust, the way they did after the foot-and-mouth outbreaks.
S3.think: Five years is enough time for me to talk myself out of doing anything. I'd keep thinking robots can't manage farrowing until the day they can.
S3.do: Saves about fifty a month and asks her uncle straight out about his plans. Looks at a veterinary nursing course at the college in year two.
S3.feel: Anxious, more than the slow picture and less than the two-year one.
S3.quote: I'd rather hear it at the kitchen table than from my cousin in the pub.
S3.fieldNote: She knows her own habit of putting things off and names it before I could. Veterinary nursing is the only switch she considers, and it is built on what she already does with sick pigs. With five years, she is willing to ask her uncle a hard question she would usually avoid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. We call this one AGI by 2036.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to sort it, so let's not get hysterical. I'd want the government to fund courses for people like me, without making it a big political fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably wait too long. Ten years sounds like forever, and I've never changed anything until I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on in the farrowing house for a few years and keep saving. Around year four or five, I'd do the vet nursing course part-time. I'd probably also learn to use the camera system if Uncle Ray buys one, because at least then I'd understand what's replacing me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not much more. It's the furthest one away, so it hurts the least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would call you out for waiting too long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum. She'd say, Uma, you said that about your driving test, and it took you four years. She'd be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In every picture so far, you start by waiting. Is that a pattern?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I suppose so. If you put it that way, I'm only safe in the boring one, and I'm not sure I believe in the boring one either.

S4.say: I'd say there's time to sort it, so let's not get hysterical. The government should fund courses for people like me without turning it into a political fight.
S4.think: I'd probably wait too long, because ten years sounds like forever. I've never changed anything until I had to.
S4.do: Keeps working in the farrowing house for a few years while saving. Takes a part-time vet nursing course around year four or five and learns the sow camera system if her uncle buys one.
S4.feel: Uneasy but not much more, because it's the furthest away.
S4.quote: I'm only safe in the boring one, and I'm not sure I believe in the boring one either.
S4.fieldNote: In every scenario she starts by waiting, and she recognised that pattern when I named it. The long warning comforts her but she expects to waste some of it. Veterinary nursing stays her one realistic plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd have no time and no money, and no idea what to train for. What would help is somebody giving farm workers real notice and a paid course in something with animals, so we're not all fighting for the same supermarket jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about family farms. Everyone thinks working for family is safe. It isn't, not when there's a bank loan and a cousin who'll inherit.

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: That's all right. I'd better get back, there's a sow due tonight.

headlineQuote: I'm family, but I'm not the family that inherits.
portrait: Uma is a 27-year-old stockperson on her uncle's pig and arable farm, sharing a house with a friend and holding about two weeks of savings. She keeps paper records because the farm's computer feeder has failed her, and she has never used an AI tool. Pragmatic and middle-of-the-road, she distrusts loud voices on every side and blames nobody in particular. Across the scenarios she starts by waiting, and she admits it. Her real fear is that being family doesn't protect her, and her only plan B is veterinary nursing.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI scenario, because she would have no time, no money and no idea what to train for.
whatWouldHelp: Real notice for farm workers and a paid course in work with animals, so they aren't all chasing the same shop jobs.
